findings.title: No in-process multi-shard test is possible today; shard logic lives in un-importable bin crates
findings.detail: All five shards (system/planet/ship/galaxy/stub) are declared as `[[bin]]` only with no `[lib]` target, and their entire game logic — including all handoff/boundary-crossing/observer-promotion ECS systems — lives in monolithic main.rs files (system-shard 7200+, ship-shard 9600+, planet-shard 3600+ lines). There is NO exported `build_app`/`spawn_shard`/`register_systems` function anywhere (grep returned zero hits). A Rust integration test physically cannot import a shard's systems to build an App in-process. The only way to exercise transfer logic is to run the compiled binaries as OS processes (k3d or local provisioner). This is the root architectural cause of untestable transfers.
findings.evidence: system-shard/planet-shard/ship-shard/galaxy-shard/stub-shard Cargo.toml all `[[bin]]` path=src/main.rs, no [lib]; grep build_app|spawn_shard|register_systems = 0 hits

findings.title: ShardHarness binds real OS sockets + real orchestrator HTTP; has no in-memory/loopback mode
findings.detail: `ShardHarness::run_ecs` unconditionally calls `start_networking()`, which binds real TCP, UDP, and QUIC sockets, spawns a healthz HTTP server, and POSTs to a real orchestrator URL to register and fetch the universe epoch (harness.rs:399-741, 903-949). There is no constructor variant that injects in-memory channels or a fake peer registry/orchestrator. Therefore even if shard systems were importable, the harness forces real network I/O and a live orchestrator into every test, defeating determinism and in-process assertions. `ShardHarness::new` is called only from the 5 shard main.rs files — never from a test.
findings.evidence: shard-common/src/harness.rs:397-741 (start_networking binds tcp/udp/quic + healthz + heartbeat), :903 register_with_orchestrator; grep ShardHarness::new shows only main.rs callers

findings.title: The core transfer state machine is untested; only the QUIC wire and one pure helper are reachable
findings.detail: handoff_pipeline.rs (145 lines) is a thin wrapper: send_handoff/send_handoff_accepted just serialize a ShardMsg onto quic_send, and build_post_handoff_redirect is a pure function picking ShardHandoff-vs-ShardRedirect (the documented 'single source of truth' for the seamless-vs-legacy choice). The actual transfer logic — boundary detection, process_handoffs, process_connects, observer promotion, source-demote countdown, pending-warp-arrival maps, hull-exit detection — all lives inside the shard main.rs ECS systems and has ZERO tests. Even build_post_handoff_redirect, which is trivially unit-testable, has no test. quic_integration.rs only proves a PlayerHandoff struct survives a loopback QUIC round-trip; it never drives the handoff handler.
findings.evidence: shard-common/src/handoff_pipeline.rs:33,89,128; shard-common/tests/quic_integration.rs (transport-only); planet-shard/src/main.rs:465-543 handoff structs are private to the bin

findings.title: Zero fault injection and zero deterministic time control anywhere in the codebase
findings.detail: Grep for packet loss, reorder, fault injection, chaos, latency injection, netem, mock clock, tokio::time::pause/advance/start_paused, manual/step tick — all returned zero relevant hits (only unrelated 'jitter' in galaxy gen and input-smoothing comments). The harness tick loop is a hard real-time `tokio::time::interval(50ms)` driving `app.update()` (harness.rs:832-876); there is no way to single-step ticks, pause virtual time, or assert state at tick N. The QUIC circuit breaker can be exercised (quic_integration.rs:152) but only by connecting to a dead port — there is no programmable loss/reorder/latency layer. Testing 'shard crash mid-transfer' or 'HandoffAccepted reply lost' is impossible without manual kubectl pod kills.
findings.evidence: grep packet.loss|reorder|fault.inject|tokio::time::pause|advance_time|step_tick = 0 relevant hits; harness.rs:834 interval(50ms), :850 app.update()

findings.title: e2e TestCluster spawns only orchestrator+gateway, never a shard, and tests admit it
findings.detail: e2e-tests/test_cluster.rs starts exactly two child processes (orchestrator in --provisioner-mode local, gateway) on random ports and waits for the /shards HTTP endpoint. It never starts a shard. orchestrator_api.rs only asserts HTTP-API contracts (register/lookup/idempotency) and explicitly comments 'can't spawn stub-shard in test env… We test the API contract, not the spawning' and accepts 200/500/504 alike. So the single integration-test harness that exists cannot place even one player on a shard, let alone observe a transfer.
findings.evidence: e2e-tests/src/test_cluster.rs:18-77 (only orchestrator+gateway); e2e-tests/tests/orchestrator_api.rs:16-24 comment + tri-state status assert

findings.title: FakeClient is a TCP stub with no transfer-following capability; stale relative to QUIC observer model
findings.detail: e2e-tests/fake_client.rs is ~47 lines: connect TCP, send ClientMsg::Connect, recv one ServerMsg. It cannot follow a ShardRedirect/ShardHandoff to a second shard, cannot hold the observer connections to nearby shards that the T0/T1 model requires, cannot send PlayerInput over UDP, and cannot assert 'I see entity X exactly once.' The gateway client path is still TCP (gateway/main.rs:9,41 TcpListener; client uses ClientMsg::Connect with ship_join_key, which still exists), so the stub isn't dead code, but it models none of the multi-connection observer-promotion behavior that transfers depend on. It is far from a scripted boundary-crossing driver.
findings.evidence: e2e-tests/src/fake_client.rs:14-46; gateway/src/main.rs:9,41,97-113; client/src/net/network.rs observer/ShardHandoff handling not mirrored in fake client

findings.title: The one 'cross-shard e2e' test proves transfers CAN be made testable — by extracting pure logic
findings.detail: shard-common/tests/chat_flow_e2e.rs:161 'cross_shard_chat_via_antenna_pair…e2e' simulates two shards entirely in-memory: it hand-builds two SignalChannelTable structs (Shard A / Shard B), runs a publish through the TX antenna, manually hands the HMAC-signed MediaFrame across the 'wire', and validates RX ingress — all with plain function calls, no processes, no sockets. The signal subsystem was deliberately extracted into the voxeldust-signal lib crate, which is why it has 172 test fns. This is the proof-of-pattern: the transfer subsystem needs the same library extraction to become deterministically testable. The capability gap is structural, not conceptual.
findings.evidence: shard-common/tests/chat_flow_e2e.rs:161-336 (in-memory two-shard sim); signal/Cargo.toml rationale comment; signal crate 172 test fns vs 0 handoff tests

findings.title: Strong unit-test coverage exists for PURE logic, establishing a reusable testing idiom
findings.detail: core has 383 test fns across 38 files, signal 172, client 64, shard-common 87 (but those 87 are signal/media/metrics/transport — not transfer). The shards' own inline #[cfg(test)] modules only cover pure helpers: arg parsing (system-shard:7201+), surface-frame reanchor math (planet-shard:3600+), seat-config roundtrips (ship-shard:9533+). The team clearly knows how to test pure functions deterministically; the problem is that transfer logic was never written as pure functions — it was written as stateful ECS systems wired directly to live network channels.
findings.evidence: test fn counts: core 383, signal 172, shard-common 87, client 64; shard inline tests at system-shard:7201, planet-shard:3600, ship-shard:9533 cover only pure helpers

findings.title: All transfer validation is manual via dev-cluster.sh + in-game client + log reading
findings.detail: dev-cluster.sh is pure k3d/docker/kubectl orchestration: build 7 images, import into k3d, apply manifests, then launch a real Bevy client and read pod logs. The harness comment in NetworkBridge (harness.rs:43-56) is itself a manual-debugging post-mortem: 'Verified end-to-end against shard-1001 logs (no player entered ship log post-handoff) and client logs (WS entities count drops by 1).' This is direct evidence the only feedback loop for transfer bugs is: rebuild images, redeploy, fly a client across a boundary, grep logs. Iteration time is minutes-to-tens-of-minutes per attempt, with no regression protection.
findings.evidence: dev-cluster.sh:49-130 (docker build/k3d import/kubectl apply/rollout); harness.rs:43-56 'Verified end-to-end against shard-1001 logs'

findings.title: No assertion primitive for the key transfer invariant: entity exists exactly-once across shards
findings.detail: The user's known bugs (eviction landmine / FIX-1, ship-exit hull trap, ping-pong handoff) are all violations of cross-shard entity-cardinality and pose-continuity invariants. There is no test scaffold that can query two shards' WorldState simultaneously and assert an entity appears on exactly one (or, during overlap, on both with consistent pose). WorldState is broadcast over UDP from inside the harness (harness.rs:477-500) with no test tap. Capturing it requires a real UDP client. So the very class of bug that hurts the user has no automated detector.
findings.evidence: harness.rs:477-500 (UDP broadcast drainer, no test hook); commits 5b78136 'Not fully working shard transfers', FIX-1 eviction (referenced in NetworkBridge doc), planet-shard:148-150 'ping-pong handoff loop … stuck between' comment

findings.title: Local provisioner spawns shards as OS child processes — usable for a process-level harness, not in-process
findings.detail: orchestrator LocalProvisioner::start_shard does Command::new(binary).spawn() with stdout/stderr inherited (provisioner.rs:57-84). This means a future test COULD drive real shard binaries as children against a real orchestrator and a scriptable QUIC/UDP fake client — a 'process-level' transfer harness — without k3d/docker. But it is still non-deterministic (real wall-clock 20Hz, real sockets, no fault injection) and the existing TestCluster does not use it for shards. It is a partial salvage path, not a deterministic one.
findings.evidence: orchestrator/src/provisioner.rs:57-84 LocalProvisioner spawns child processes; orchestrator/src/config.rs:40-42 provisioner_mode=local default

summary:
Transfer-testing capability rating: 1/10. A multi-shard topology CANNOT run in-process for a deterministic integration test today. Testing any transfer requires the k3d cluster (or, at best, real OS child-process shards) plus manual in-game client checks and log-grepping — exactly the user's pain.

Three compounding architectural blockers:
1. Shards are bin-only crates (no [lib]); all transfer logic (boundary detection, process_handoffs, process_connects, observer promotion, source-demote, hull-exit) is buried in 3,600–9,600-line main.rs ECS systems that no test can import. There is no build_app/spawn_shard export anywhere.
2. ShardHarness::run_ecs unconditionally binds real TCP/UDP/QUIC sockets and registers with a live orchestrator over HTTP. It has no in-memory/loopback mode and is never instantiated from a test — only from the 5 shard mains.
3. The tick loop is hard real-time tokio::time::interval(50ms); there is zero deterministic time control (no pause/advance/step) and zero fault injection (no packet loss/reorder/latency/crash hooks) anywhere in the repo.

What exists: 383 core + 172 signal pure unit tests; a QUIC transport round-trip test (struct survives loopback); an orchestrator HTTP-contract e2e (TestCluster spawns only orchestrator+gateway, never a shard, and admits it); a TCP FakeClient stub that can send one Connect and read one ServerMsg but cannot follow a redirect/handoff, hold observer connections, send input, or assert entity cardinality. The lone 'cross-shard' test (chat_flow_e2e) is an in-memory two-struct simulation — and that is precisely the pattern to copy: the signal subsystem was extracted into a lib crate and is deeply tested; transfers were not.

Rebuild's first milestone must be a transfer harness. Its hard prerequisites that today's structure PREVENTS: (a) extract handoff/boundary/observer logic into a pure, side-effect-free lib crate (like voxeldust-signal); (b) make the harness injectable — in-memory channels + fake peer registry/orchestrator instead of forced sockets; (c) deterministic clock with manual tick stepping; (d) a programmable transport layer for loss/reorder/latency/crash; (e) a scriptable fake client that holds N observer connections and follows redirects; (f) an assertion API over multiple shards' WorldState (entity-exists-exactly-once, pose continuity).</summary>
<open_questions>["Does the client's observer/ShardHandoff promotion logic (client/src/net/network.rs, connection.rs) have any unit coverage, or is the client side of transfers equally manual? (client crate has 64 test fns but unclear if any touch transfer flow)","Is the gateway-to-client transport intentionally still TCP while inter-shard is QUIC, and does a transfer harness need to model the gateway hop or can it connect a fake client directly to shard TCP/UDP?","Are PlayerHandoff/HandoffAccepted/ShardHandoff structs already in the shared core/handoff.rs lib (testable) while only the *handlers* are trapped in bins — confirming the extraction is handler-only, not data-model?","Does the local provisioner path actually launch real shard binaries successfully outside k3d (it spawns Command::new(binary)), making a process-level harness a quicker stopgap than full logic extraction?"]</open_questions>
<rebuild_implications>Keep-and-harden is NOT viable for the transfer subsystem's testability: the bin-only structure and socket-coupled harness mean no amount of patching yields a deterministic transfer test. This strongly favors a rebuild-from-scratch-transfer-first approach that keeps the multi-shard CONCEPT but restructures for testability. The very first milestone must be the transfer harness itself, built before re-implementing transfer features: (1) a voxeldust-transfer (or shard-core) lib crate holding the handoff/observer/boundary state machine as pure functions over plain state, mirroring how voxeldust-signal was extracted; (2) shards refactored to thin bins that wire the lib to I/O; (3) an injectable harness taking in-memory mpsc channels + a trait-object PeerRegistry/Orchestrator/Transport so a test can spawn N shard 'cores' in one process; (4) a deterministic virtual clock (tokio start_paused or an explicit step_tick API) replacing the hard 50ms interval; (5) a fault-injecting in-memory transport (drop/reorder/delay/partition + crash-a-shard-mid-handoff); (6) a scriptable fake client modeling multi-shard observer connections and redirect-following; (7) multi-shard assertion helpers (entity-exactly-once, pose-continuity, no-ghost-after-demote) that directly target the user's known bug classes (eviction landmine, hull trap, ping-pong). Build this harness first, then port transfer features into it test-driven.</rebuild_implications>
